claim: In budding yeast, ~35% of all TFs are associated with a single WGD event dating back to ~100 million years ago.
source: In budding yeast, ~35% of all TFs are associated with a single WGD event dating back to ~100 million years ago (Figure 1A; Wolfe and Shields, 1997; Marcet-Houben and Gabaldón, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Wolfe and Shields, 1997; Marcet-Houben and Gabaldón, 2015) and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Within the Saccharomyces cerevisiae genome database (SGD), 82 proteins containing an annotated DNA-binding domain (DBD) are classified as WGD-retained paralogs.
source: Within the Saccharomyces cerevisiae genome database (SGD) (Cherry et al., 2012), 82 proteins containing an annotated DNA-binding domain (DBD) are classified as WGD-retained paralogs (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the SGD database (Cherry et al., 2012) and reference to Figure 1A and B.

claim: A total of 30 pairs (60 TFs) were successfully profiled using ChEC-seq.
source: A total of 30 pairs (60 TFs) were successfully profiled, as verified by data reproducibility (Pearson's r>0.95 in promoter-binding preferences, Figure 1C) and manual literature survey (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing reproducibility (Pearson's r>0.95) and reference to figures showing the profiling results.

claim: Binding preferences were conserved (Pearson's r>0.8) among ~40% of paralogs.
source: Perhaps unexpectedly, binding preferences were conserved (Pearson's r>0.8) among ~40% of paralogs, most notably these of the C2H2 zinc finger family (e.g. Met31/Met32, Figure 1D, 6/10 pairs Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation data (Pearson's r>0.8) and reference to specific examples in figures.

claim: Most diverging paralogs still shared a substantial fraction of target promoters.
source: Furthermore, most diverging paralogs still shared a substantial fraction of target promoters (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2 showing target promoter overlap.

claim: In some cases, the two duplicates localized to the same promoters but with different relative strengths.
source: In some cases, the two duplicates localized to the same promoters but with different relative strengths (e.g. Gzf3/Dal80, Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by a specific example (Gzf3/Dal80) shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In other cases, some promoters were bound by both paralogs, while others were preferentially bound by just one paralog.
source: In other cases, some promoters were bound by both paralogs, while others were preferentially bound by just one paralog (e.g. Ace2/Swi5, Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by a specific example (Ace2/Swi5) shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Specificity-conferring residues often varied between paralogs of the fungal-specific zinc cluster family.
source: In particular, specificity-conferring residues often varied between paralogs of the fungal-specific zinc cluster family (Figure 3B), but remained invariant between paralogs of the C2H2 zinc finger family (e.g. Rph1/Gis1) and, to a lesser extent, other families (e.g. Dot6/Tod6, Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Specificity-conferring residues remained invariant between paralogs of the C2H2 zinc finger family.
source: In particular, specificity-conferring residues often varied between paralogs of the fungal-specific zinc cluster family (Figure 3B), but remained invariant between paralogs of the C2H2 zinc finger family (e.g. Rph1/Gis1) and, to a lesser extent, other families (e.g. Dot6/Tod6, Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 3A and B, with specific example Rph1/Gis1.

claim: DBD-swapping perturbed promoter binding for three of the four zinc cluster TFs tested.
source: Consistent with their strong DBD sequence divergence, DBD-swapping perturbed promoter binding for three of the four zinc cluster TFs tested.
evidence: The claim is supported by DBD-swapping experimental results.

claim: In none of the zinc cluster TFs was DBD-swapping sufficient for switching promoter preferences to those of the paralog from which the DBD was taken.
source: However, in none of these was DBD-swapping sufficient for switching promoter preferences to those of the paralog from which the DBD was taken (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by DBD-swapping experimental results shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: In all other 12 cases studied, binding preferences remained largely invariant to the swapping of the DBD (Pearson's r>0.8).
source: Further, in all other 12 cases studied, binding preferences remained largely invariant to the swapping of the DBD (Pearson's r>0.8).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation data (Pearson's r>0.8) from DBD-swapping experiments.

claim: For most paralog pairs, the variations driving divergence in promoter-binding preferences are located outside the DBDs.
source: We conclude that, for most paralog pairs, the variations driving divergence in promoter-binding preferences are located outside the DBDs.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the DBD-swapping experimental results.

claim: Two TFs completely lost binding signals (Pip2, Hms2) upon paralog deletion.
source: Two TFs completely lost binding signals (Pip2, Hms2) upon paralog deletion, and additional two lost binding to their respective paralogs' targets (Dal80, Tbs1).
evidence: The claim is supported by paralog deletion experimental data.

claim: Additional two TFs lost binding to their respective paralogs' targets (Dal80, Tbs1) upon paralog deletion.
source: Two TFs completely lost binding signals (Pip2, Hms2) upon paralog deletion, and additional two lost binding to their respective paralogs' targets (Dal80, Tbs1).
evidence: The claim is supported by paralog deletion experimental data.

claim: Large-scale effects of paralog deletion were infrequent.
source: These large-scale effects, however, were infrequent (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B and C from paralog deletion experiments.

claim: Cooperative interactions between TF paralogs were generally minor.
source: In fact, cooperative interactions were generally minor (e.g. Stp2), as were compensatory interactions (e.g. Pdr3 or Ecm22; Figure 5C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from paralog deletion experiments shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Compensatory interactions between TF paralogs were generally minor.
source: In fact, cooperative interactions were generally minor (e.g. Stp2), as were compensatory interactions (e.g. Pdr3 or Ecm22; Figure 5C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from paralog deletion experiments shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Strong interactions between TF paralogs are rare and existing ones tend to increase mutation fragility.
source: Therefore, strong interactions between TF paralogs are rare and existing ones tend to increase mutation fragility.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the paralog deletion experimental results.

claim: Paralogs of the C2H2 zinc finger family evolved symmetrically, consistent with sub-functionalization.
source: We observe that paralogs of the C2H2 zinc finger family, including the diverging ones, evolved symmetrically, that is, at rates that did not distinguish between paralogs, consistent with sub-functionalization (e.g. Tda9/Rsf2 and Gis1/Rph1, Figure 6C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic sequence analysis data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Diverging paralogs of other families evolved asymmetrically, suggesting dominant neo-functionalization.
source: By contrast, diverging paralogs of other families evolved asymmetrically, suggesting dominant neo-functionalization (e.g. Vhr1/Vhr2, Figure 6C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic sequence analysis data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: The binding preferences of Ixr1/Abf2's K. lactis ortholog were indistinguishable from these of Ixr1.
source: We find that the binding preferences of Ixr1/Abf2's K. lactis ortholog were indistinguishable from these of Ixr1 (Figure 7A), consistent with Abf2's accelerated sequence evolution (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by binding profile data shown in Figure 7A and sequence evolution data in Figure 6B.

claim: K. lactis orthologs of paralogs with non-diverged binding preferences retained highly similar preferences.
source: Similarly, K. lactis orthologs of paralogs with non-diverged binding preferences retained highly similar preferences, for example, Rsf2/Tda9 regulators of respiration-related functions (Figure 7B and C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1 for additional pairs).
evidence: The claim is supported by binding profile data shown in Figure 7B, C, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In all 11 diverging cases, binding preference similarity of at least one paralog with the K. lactis ortholog exceeded the similarity with the other S. cerevisiae paralog.
source: Of note, in all 11 diverging cases, binding preference similarity of at least one paralog with the K. lactis ortholog exceeded the similarity with the other S. cerevisiae paralog.
evidence: The claim is supported by binding profile comparison data from K. lactis ortholog experiments.

claim: In nine of the diverging cases, the sequence of the paralog with the more conserved binding profile was also slower to evolve.
source: In nine of these cases, the sequence of the paralog with the more conserved binding profile was also slower to evolve (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by combined binding profile and sequence evolution data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The prevalent route for diversification appears to comply with a biased neo/sub-functionalization: ancestral preferences split unevenly between the duplicates, coupled to biased acquisition of novel targets.
source: The prevalent route for diversification therefore appears to comply with a biased neo/sub-functionalization: ancestral preferences split unevenly between the duplicates, coupled to biased acquisition of novel targets (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the K. lactis ortholog binding profile data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In three of the five diverging zinc cluster pairs, differences in binding preferences correlated with differential motif preferences.
source: In three of the five diverging pairs, differences in binding preferences correlated with differential motif preferences (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1): Hal9/Tbs1 and Oaf1/Pip2 showing differential spacing/orientation and Pdr1/Pdr3 showing variation within the CGG.
evidence: The claim is supported by motif analysis data shown in Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Hal9/Tbs1 recruited each other to their preferred sites, likely through heterodimerization.
source: All three pairs interacted: Hal9/Tbs1 recruited each other to their preferred sites, likely through heterodimerization, and Pip2 localized exclusively to a subset of Oaf1-preferred targets in an Oaf1-dependent manner, consistent with obligatory heterodimerization (Rottensteiner et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by binding data and inference about mechanism, with citation to supporting literature (Rottensteiner et al., 1997).

claim: Pip2 localized exclusively to a subset of Oaf1-preferred targets in an Oaf1-dependent manner, consistent with obligatory heterodimerization.
source: All three pairs interacted: Hal9/Tbs1 recruited each other to their preferred sites, likely through heterodimerization, and Pip2 localized exclusively to a subset of Oaf1-preferred targets in an Oaf1-dependent manner, consistent with obligatory heterodimerization (Rottensteiner et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by binding data and citation to supporting literature (Rottensteiner et al., 1997).

claim: In the case of Pdr1/Pdr3, interaction took the form of competition, with Pdr1 outcompeting Pdr3 from accessing its preferred binding sites.
source: In the case of Pdr1/Pdr3, interaction took the form of competition, with Pdr1 outcompeting Pdr3 from accessing its preferred binding sites (Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is supported by binding data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: CGG-containing motifs at Yrr1/Pdr8- or Upc2/Ecm22-bound sites did not distinguish between paralogs.
source: Contrasting these, CGG-containing motifs at Yrr1/Pdr8- or Upc2/Ecm22-bound sites did not distinguish between paralogs (Figure 8A–D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif analysis data shown in Figure 8A–D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Yrr1/Pdr8 paralogs localized to the same motifs, but within different promoters.
source: Rather, paralogs localized to the same motifs, but within different promoters.
evidence: The claim is supported by binding and motif analysis data.

claim: The divergence of promoter preferences for Yrr1/Pdr8 was largely DBD-independent.
source: This divergence of promoter preferences was largely DBD-independent in the case of Yrr1/Pdr8 (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by DBD-swapping experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the case of Upc2/Ecm22, divergence of promoter preferences was largely DBD-dependent competition.
source: In the case of Upc2/Ecm22, on the other hand, it was largely DBD-dependent competition (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by DBD-swapping and competition experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Upon UPC2 deletion or DBD-swapping, Ecm22 gained access to strong Upc2 sites.
source: In fact, upon UPC2 deletion or DBD-swapping, Ecm22 gained access to strong Upc2 sites (Figure 8C–E; note correspondence to K. lactis sites).
evidence: The claim is supported by deletion and DBD-swapping experimental data shown in Figure 8C–E.

claim: While DBD-swapping retained binding at the TF-specific sites, it also allowed increased access to non-specific sites, suggesting co-evolution of the DBD and the linker domain.
source: Of note, while DBD-swapping retained binding at the TF-specific sites, it also allowed increased access to non-specific sites, suggesting co-evolution of the DBD and the linker domain, both of which varied substantially between the paralogs (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by DBD-swapping experimental data and inference about co-evolution, with citation to supporting literature (Yang et al., 2015).

claim: Zinc cluster paralogs evolved largely, but not exclusively, through changes in motif preferences or affinity, resulting from combined effects of variations within, and outside, their DBDs.
source: We conclude that zinc cluster paralogs evolved largely, but not exclusively, through changes in motif preferences or affinity, resulting from combined effects of variations within, and outside, their DBDs.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the combined analysis of zinc cluster paralogs.

claim: Rph1 gained residual access to Gis1-binding sites upon GIS1 deletion or DBD-swapping.
source: We noted, however, that Rph1 gained residual access to Gis1-binding sites upon GIS1 deletion or DBD-swapping (Figure 9A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by deletion and DBD-swapping experimental data shown in Figure 9A and B.

claim: Rph1-exclusive targets contained a specific variant of the common Gis1/Rph1 motif, lacking from Gis1-binding sites.
source: Further, Rph1-exclusive targets contained a specific variant of the common Gis1/Rph1 motif, lacking from Gis1-binding sites (Figure 9C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif analysis data shown in Figure 9C and D.

claim: Gis1 has lost a conserved demethylase activity, an event that occurred quite soon following WGD.
source: Phylogenetic analysis revealed two sequence variations between the paralogs: first, Gis1 has lost a conserved demethylase activity (Klose et al., 2006), an event that occurred quite soon following WGD.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis and citation to supporting literature (Klose et al., 2006).

claim: Rph1's DBD experienced a more recent (minor) variation altering a conserved residue.
source: Second, Rph1's DBD experienced a more recent (minor) variation altering a conserved residue (Figure 9E and Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in Figure 9E and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: A loss of demethylase activity allowed Gis1 to specialize toward a subset of (weaker) ancestral targets and acquire new binding sites, through a primarily DBD-independent evolution.
source: Together, this suggests the following evolutionary scenario: first, a loss of demethylase activity allowed Gis1 to specialize toward a subset of (weaker) ancestral targets and acquire new binding sites, through a primarily DBD-independent evolution.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the combined phylogenetic and binding data.

claim: Mutations within Rph1's DBD prevented its binding to Gis1-specialized sites, thereby reducing paralog interference.
source: Second, mutations within Rph1's DBD prevented its binding to Gis1-specialized sites, thereby reducing paralog interference (Figure 9E).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the combined phylogenetic and binding data shown in Figure 9E.

claim: Other diverging paralogs whose K. lactis orthologs were profiled appear to conform to a general model where DBD-independent divergence is complemented by asymmetric competition, limiting residual paralog interference.
source: Extending the analysis to other diverging paralogs pointed at additional cases which might conform to this same design whereby limited binding competition resolved residual paralog interference (Figure 9F and Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the analysis of multiple paralog pairs shown in Figure 9F and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: A common path for divergence is whereby DBD-independent divergence is complemented by asymmetric competition, limiting residual paralog interference.
source: Together, these results suggest a common path, whereby DBD-independent divergence is complemented by asymmetric competition, limiting residual paralog interference.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the combined analysis of multiple paralog pairs.

claim: ~60% of WGD-retained TF paralogs evolved differential binding preferences.
source: Using high-resolution profiling, we find that ~60% of paralogs evolved differential binding preferences.
evidence: The claim is supported by high-resolution profiling data from the study.

claim: The divergence of binding preferences among WGD TF paralogs results primarily from variations outside the DNA-binding domains (DBDs).
source: We show that this divergence results primarily from variations outside the DNA-binding domains (DBDs), while DBD preferences remain largely conserved.
evidence: The claim is supported by DBD-swapping experimental data and sequence analysis.

claim: DBD preferences remain largely conserved among WGD TF paralogs.
source: We show that this divergence results primarily from variations outside the DNA-binding domains (DBDs), while DBD preferences remain largely conserved.
evidence: The claim is supported by DBD-swapping experimental data and sequence analysis.

claim: Analysis of non-WGD orthologs revealed uneven splitting of ancestral preferences between duplicates.
source: Analysis of non-WGD orthologs revealed uneven splitting of ancestral preferences between duplicates, and the preferential acquiring of new targets by the least conserved paralog (biased neo/sub-functionalization).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of K. lactis ortholog binding profiles.

claim: The least conserved paralog preferentially acquires new targets (biased neo/sub-functionalization).
source: Analysis of non-WGD orthologs revealed uneven splitting of ancestral preferences between duplicates, and the preferential acquiring of new targets by the least conserved paralog (biased neo/sub-functionalization).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of K. lactis ortholog binding profiles and sequence evolution data.

claim: Interactions between paralogs were rare.
source: Interactions between paralogs were rare, and, when present, occurred through weak competition for DNA-binding or dependency between dimer-forming paralogs.
evidence: The claim is supported by paralog deletion experimental data.

claim: When present, interactions between paralogs occurred through weak competition for DNA-binding or dependency between dimer-forming paralogs.
source: Interactions between paralogs were rare, and, when present, occurred through weak competition for DNA-binding or dependency between dimer-forming paralogs.
evidence: The claim is supported by paralog deletion experimental data.

claim: Gene duplication is the major source of new TFs.
source: Gene duplication is the major source of new TFs (Ohno et al., 1968; Rosanova et al., 2017; Vaquerizas et al., 2009; Levine and Tjian, 2003; Teichmann and Babu, 2004), with whole-genome duplications (WGDs) playing a particularly important role (Blanc and Wolfe, 2004; Maere et al., 2005; Rody et al., 2017; Wolfe and Shields, 1997; Marcet-Houben and Gabaldón, 2015; Birchler et al., 2005; Freeling and Thomas, 2006; Edger and Pires, 2009; Lundin, 1993; Dehal and Boore, 2005; Blomme et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Whole-genome duplications (WGDs) play a particularly important role in generating new TFs.
source: Gene duplication is the major source of new TFs (Ohno et al., 1968; Rosanova et al., 2017; Vaquerizas et al., 2009; Levine and Tjian, 2003; Teichmann and Babu, 2004), with whole-genome duplications (WGDs) playing a particularly important role (Blanc and Wolfe, 2004; Maere et al., 2005; Rody et al., 2017; Wolfe and Shields, 1997; Marcet-Houben and Gabaldón, 2015; Birchler et al., 2005; Freeling and Thomas, 2006; Edger and Pires, 2009; Lundin, 1993; Dehal and Boore, 2005; Blomme et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Different TFs that bind to similar DNA sequences in vitro localize to different genomic sites in vivo through poorly understood mechanisms.
source: For example, different TFs that bind to similar DNA sequences in vitro (Weirauch et al., 2014; Wei et al., 2010; Jolma et al., 2013; Matys et al., 2006; Siggers et al., 2014; Nakagawa et al., 2013; Rogers and Bulyk, 2018; Berger et al., 2008; Shen et al., 2018) localize to different genomic sites in vivo through poorly understood mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: TF duplicates (paralogs) can diverge through changes in expression, regulation, or function.
source: TF duplicates (paralogs) can diverge through changes in expression, regulation, or function (Vavouri et al., 2008; DeLuna et al., 2008; Diss et al., 2014; Kafri et al., 2006; Wapinski et al., 2007; Gu et al., 2003; VanderSluis et al., 2010; Charoensawan et al., 2010; Des Marais and Rausher, 2008; Hsiao and Vitkup, 2008; Ihmels et al., 2007; Kuzmin et al., 2020; Ehrenreich, 2020; Payne and Wagner, 2015; Chen et al., 2013; Burga et al., 2011; Macneil and Walhout, 2011; Diss et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Mechanisms driving divergence of TF-binding sites include changes in co-factor binding.
source: Mechanisms driving divergence of TF-binding sites include changes in co-factor binding (Baker et al., 2013) or in DNA motif preferences (Pérez et al., 2014; Blake and Barolo, 2014; McKeown et al., 2014; Bridgham et al., 2008; Humbert et al., 2013; Pougach et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Baker et al., 2013).

claim: Mechanisms driving divergence of TF-binding sites include changes in DNA motif preferences.
source: Mechanisms driving divergence of TF-binding sites include changes in co-factor binding (Baker et al., 2013) or in DNA motif preferences (Pérez et al., 2014; Blake and Barolo, 2014; McKeown et al., 2014; Bridgham et al., 2008; Humbert et al., 2013; Pougach et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: A large fraction of TFs were bound at their own or their paralog's promoters, potentially forming regulatory circuits.
source: A large fraction of TFs were bound at their own or their paralog's promoters, potentially forming regulatory circuits (Figure 1E; Teichmann and Babu, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by binding data shown in Figure 1E and citation to supporting literature (Teichmann and Babu, 2004).

claim: TFs of the zinc cluster family bind DNA as dimers, recognizing a composite DNA motif that includes two spaced CGG sites.
source: TFs of this family bind DNA as dimers, recognizing a composite DNA motif that includes two spaced CGG sites (MacPherson et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (MacPherson et al., 2006).

claim: Binding specificity of zinc cluster TFs depends on the orientation of the DBD-bound CGG triplets, and on the spacer length, which likely relates to the unstructured linker flanking the DBD.
source: Binding specificity depends on the orientation of the DBD-bound CGG triplets, and on the spacer length, which likely relates to the unstructured linker flanking the DBD (Figure 8A; Reece and Ptashne, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 8A and citation to published literature (Reece and Ptashne, 1993).

claim: Compared to other families, divergence of zinc cluster paralogs was more dependent on DBD variations.
source: Compared to other families, divergence of zinc cluster paralogs was more dependent on DBD variations (Figure 4C), and these paralogs were more likely to interact (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by DBD-swapping data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Zinc cluster paralogs were more likely to interact compared to other families.
source: Compared to other families, divergence of zinc cluster paralogs was more dependent on DBD variations (Figure 4C), and these paralogs were more likely to interact (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by paralog deletion data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Binding preferences of both Hal9/Tbs1 heterodimers correlated well with that of the K. lactis ortholog.
source: Notably, binding preferences of both heterodimers correlated well with that of the K. lactis ortholog (Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is supported by binding profile comparison data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: A neo-functionalizing paralog undergoes a period of relaxed selection, followed by rapid evolution, and is therefore expected to evolve at an accelerated rate.
source: This analysis is informative, since a neo-functionalizing paralog undergoes a period of relaxed selection, followed by rapid evolution, and is therefore expected to evolve at an accelerated rate (Pegueroles et al., 2013; Byrne and Wolfe, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Pegueroles et al., 2013; Byrne and Wolfe, 2007).

claim: Abf2 has a mitochondrial function and localization.
source: The Ixr1 and Abf2 paralogs have diverged completely, with Abf2 having a mitochondrial function and localization (MacPherson et al., 2006) and Ixr1 being a nuclear repressor regulating hypoxia genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (MacPherson et al., 2006).

claim: Ixr1 is a nuclear repressor regulating hypoxia genes.
source: The Ixr1 and Abf2 paralogs have diverged completely, with Abf2 having a mitochondrial function and localization (MacPherson et al., 2006) and Ixr1 being a nuclear repressor regulating hypoxia genes.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Ixr1 function.

claim: Rsf2/Tda9 are regulators of respiration-related functions.
source: Similarly, K. lactis orthologs of paralogs with non-diverged binding preferences retained highly similar preferences, for example, Rsf2/Tda9 regulators of respiration-related functions (Figure 7B and C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1 for additional pairs).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Rsf2/Tda9 function.

claim: Rph1 has histone demethylase activity.
source: Phylogenetic analysis revealed two sequence variations between the paralogs: first, Gis1 has lost a conserved demethylase activity (Klose et al., 2006), an event that occurred quite soon following WGD.
evidence: The claim is implied by the statement that Gis1 lost demethylase activity, and supported by citation (Klose et al., 2006).

claim: The set of WGD TF duplicates in budding yeast provides a convenient platform for studying the fate of duplicated and retained TF genes.
source: We reasoned that this set of TF duplicates, all generated at the same time and subjected to the same evolutionary history, provides a convenient platform for studying the fate of duplicated and retained TF genes.
evidence: The claim is a reasoning statement about the study design.

claim: The refined list of WGD-retained TF paralogs includes only pairs where both paralogs act as specific TFs (35 pairs).
source: We refined this list to include only pairs where both paralogs act as specific TFs (35 pairs, Supplementary file 1), and defined the binding locations of these TFs across the genome using chromatin endogenous cleavage with high-throughput sequencing (ChEC-seq) (Zentner et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim describes the study's methodology and is supported by reference to Supplementary file 1 and citation to the ChEC-seq method (Zentner et al., 2015).

claim: ChEC-seq was used to define the binding locations of TFs across the genome.
source: We refined this list to include only pairs where both paralogs act as specific TFs (35 pairs, Supplementary file 1), and defined the binding locations of these TFs across the genome using chromatin endogenous cleavage with high-throughput sequencing (ChEC-seq) (Zentner et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim describes the study's methodology and is supported by citation to the ChEC-seq method (Zentner et al., 2015).

claim: Binding preferences diverge at a rate that differs between pairs, and, within each pair, differs between individual promoters.
source: Therefore, binding preferences diverge at a rate that differs between pairs, and, within each pair, differs between individual promoters.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the binding profile data.

claim: Reported in vitro motif preferences are often similar among paralogs.
source: Examining motif preferences derived from in vitro data, we noted that reported preferences (Weirauch et al., 2014; Lambert et al., 2019) are often (although not always) similar among paralogs (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of in vitro motif data from cited sources (Weirauch et al., 2014; Lambert et al., 2019) and shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: DBD variations may contribute to the divergence of zinc cluster paralogs.
source: DBD variations may therefore contribute to the divergence of zinc cluster paralogs, but appear to play a lesser role in paralogs of the C2H2 zinc finger and perhaps other families.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from sequence analysis and DBD-swapping experiments.

claim: DBD variations appear to play a lesser role in paralogs of the C2H2 zinc finger and perhaps other families.
source: DBD variations may therefore contribute to the divergence of zinc cluster paralogs, but appear to play a lesser role in paralogs of the C2H2 zinc finger and perhaps other families.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from sequence analysis and DBD-swapping experiments.

claim: If DBD variations drive divergence, swapping DBDs would swap promoter preferences.
source: We swapped DBDs between paralogs (Figure 4A), reasoning that if DBD variations drive divergence, swapping DBDs would swap promoter preferences.
evidence: The claim is a logical reasoning statement about the experimental design.

claim: If critical variations are located outside the DBD, DBD-swapping will be of little effect.
source: Conversely, if critical variations are located outside the DBD, swapping will be of little effect.
evidence: The claim is a logical reasoning statement about the experimental design.

claim: Paralog TFs that bind DNA as dimers may bind as heterodimers to a subset of sites.
source: Paralog TFs that bind DNA as dimers, for example, may bind as heterodimers to a subset of sites.
evidence: The claim is a speculative statement about possible paralog interactions.

claim: Paralogs may compete for DNA binding, either directly or by interacting with a shared co-factor.
source: Paralogs may also compete for DNA binding, either directly or by interacting with a shared co-factor.
evidence: The claim is a speculative statement about possible paralog interactions.

claim: Cooperative interactions increase mutation fragility whereas binding competition increases mutation robustness.
source: In the broader context, cooperative interactions, where a TF becomes dependent on its paralog, may increase mutation fragility whereas binding competition, which allows a TF to access sites bound exclusively by its paralog upon the latter's perturbation, may increase mutation robustness (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is a reasoning statement about the functional consequences of paralog interactions, illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: Both cooperative and competitive effects were observed in the context of protein-protein interactions.

claim: The non-WGD ortholog might serve as a good proxy for the ancestor TF in terms of binding preferences.
source: We reasoned that, in terms of binding preferences, this non-WGD ortholog might serve as a good proxy for the ancestor TF (Teichmann and Babu, 2004; Hsia and McGinnis, 2003; Carroll, 2005).
evidence: The claim is a reasoning statement supported by citations to published literature (Teichmann and Babu, 2004; Hsia and McGinnis, 2003; Carroll, 2005).

claim: The use of non-WGD orthologs to approximate ancestral preferences is supported by experimental results.
source: Together, these results support the use of non-WGD orthologs to approximate ancestral preferences.

claim: In three of the five diverging zinc cluster pairs, binding preferences evolved through a combination of DNA-motif preferences and protein-protein interactions.
source: In these three cases described above, binding preferences evolved through a combination of DNA-motif preferences and protein-protein interactions.

claim: DBD variations may play a role in resolving residual paralog interference even when changes in motif preference are secondary.
source: Still, even in such cases, DBD variations may play a role in resolving residual paralog interference (Baker et al., 2013; Kaltenegger and Ober, 2015).
evidence: The claim is a speculative statement supported by citations to published literature (Baker et al., 2013; Kaltenegger and Ober, 2015).

claim: Divergence of binding preferences requires not only the acquisition of differential preferences, but also limiting residual paralog's cross binding.
source: Thus, since the two paralogs are initially redundant, divergence of binding preferences requires not only the acquisition of differential preferences, but also limiting residual, and possibly interfering paralog's cross binding.
evidence: The claim is a reasoning statement about the requirements for paralog divergence.

claim: In the case of the non-WGD pair Mcm1/Arg80, interference was resolved by weakening direct Arg80-DNA binding.
source: In the case of the non-WGD pair Mcm1/Arg80, for example, such interference was resolved by weakening direct Arg80-DNA binding (Baker et al., 2013; Kaltenegger and Ober, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Baker et al., 2013; Kaltenegger and Ober, 2015).

claim: In most cases of diverging TF paralogs, divergence in promoter binding is driven by variations outside the DBD, with competition only refining, but not driving this divergence of target preferences.
source: Note that in most cases (indicated), divergence in promoter binding is driven by variations outside the DBD, with competition only refining, but not driving this divergence of target preferences.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the combined analysis shown in Figure 9F.

claim: The majority of pairs of WGD-retained TF paralogs still share a large fraction of overlapping targets.
source: Studying a comprehensive set of WGD-retained TF paralogs, we found that the majority of pairs still share a large fraction of overlapping targets.
evidence: The claim is supported by binding profile data from the study.

claim: Even diverged paralogs still localized to common targets, although at different relative strengths.
source: In fact, even diverged paralogs still localized to common targets, although at different relative strengths.
evidence: The claim is supported by binding profile data from the study.

claim: This gradual divergence was not explained by variations in the DBDs.
source: This gradual divergence was not explained by variations in the DBDs.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the DBD-swapping and sequence analysis experiments.

claim: With the exception of the zinc cluster family, variations within the DBD contributed little to binding divergence.
source: In particular, we presented evidence that, with the exception of the zinc cluster family, variations within the DBD contributed little to binding divergence.
evidence: The claim is supported by DBD-swapping experimental data.

claim: DBD preferences may play a minor role in setting promoter-binding preferences but be primarily important for stabilizing binding within selected promoters.
source: DBD preferences may play a minor role in setting promoter-binding preferences but be primarily important for stabilizing binding within selected promoters.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Cooperation and competition act to adjust binding profiles and limit paralog interference but are not the major factors guiding divergence.
source: Further, cooperation and competition act to adjust binding profiles and limit paralog interference but, with few exceptions, are not the major factors guiding divergence.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the paralog deletion experimental data.

claim: Gradual, promoter-specific divergence is harder to explain within models in which TF-binding specificity depends on a single DNA-binding motif or a single recruiting factor.
source: In this context, gradual, and promoter-specific divergence is harder to explain within models in which TF-binding specificity depends on a single DNA-binding motif or a single recruiting factor.
evidence: The claim is a reasoning statement about the implications of the findings.

claim: The gradual, gene-specific divergence observed may be more naturally explained in models where binding depends on multiple specificity determinants within the TF, which recognize a corresponding multiplicity of features within the promoter.
source: The gradual, gene-specific divergence we observe may be more naturally explained in models where binding depends on multiple specificity determinants within the TF, which recognize a corresponding multiplicity of features within the promoter.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The existence of multiplicity of specificity determinants would allow to tune more readily TF binding at the level of individual promoters.
source: The existence of such multiplicity would allow to tune more readily TF binding at the level of individual promoters.
evidence: The claim is a speculative reasoning statement.

claim: Msn2 and Yap1 TFs' promoter-binding depends on the cumulative contribution of a large number of specificity determinants distributed throughout their long intrinsically disordered regions.
source: We recently described one such paradigm in the context of the Msn2 and Yap1 TFs, whose promoter-binding depends on the cumulative contribution of a large number of specificity determinants distributed throughout their long (>500 amino acids) intrinsically disordered regions (Jana et al., 2021; Brodsky et al., 2020; Brodsky et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature from the authors' lab (Jana et al., 2021; Brodsky et al., 2020; Brodsky et al., 2021).

claim: Duplication is the major means through which new TFs emerge.
source: At the more global level, since duplication is the major means through which new TFs emerge, the evolutionary trajectories of retained paralogs shape the transcriptional network's design.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The evolutionary trajectories of retained paralogs shape the transcriptional network's design.
source: At the more global level, since duplication is the major means through which new TFs emerge, the evolutionary trajectories of retained paralogs shape the transcriptional network's design.
evidence: The claim is a reasoning statement about the implications of the findings.

claim: Duplicates that diverge through sub-functionalization will confer a hierarchical design, where regulatory modules are gradually refined as the network expands.
source: Duplicates that diverge through sub-functionalization, for example, will confer a hierarchical design, where regulatory modules are gradually refined as the network expands.
evidence: The claim is a speculative reasoning statement about the implications of sub-functionalization.

claim: Neo-functionalization may support a distributed design, where new regulatory modules can emerge largely independent of previous connectivity.
source: By contrast, neo-functionalization may support a distributed design, where new regulatory modules can emerge largely independent of previous connectivity.
evidence: The claim is a speculative reasoning statement about the implications of neo-functionalization.

claim: Neo-functionalization is quite common among diverging WGD TF paralogs.
source: Focusing on the 60% diverging pairs, our results reveal that neo-functionalization is quite common, although it is often combined with a biased sub-functionalization, namely uneven splitting of ancestral targets.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of K. lactis ortholog binding profiles and sequence evolution data.

claim: Neo-functionalization is often combined with a biased sub-functionalization, namely uneven splitting of ancestral targets.
source: Focusing on the 60% diverging pairs, our results reveal that neo-functionalization is quite common, although it is often combined with a biased sub-functionalization, namely uneven splitting of ancestral targets.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of K. lactis ortholog binding profiles and sequence evolution data.

claim: A significant fraction of paralog pairs (~40%) still binds at practically identical sites.
source: Whereas we focused our analysis on diverging paralogs, it is notable that a significant fraction of paralog pairs (~40%) still binds at practically identical sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by binding profile data from the study.

claim: Retention of paralogs that bind at identical sites is due to properties other than binding divergence.
source: Retention of these paralogs is therefore due to other properties.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observation that some paralogs have identical binding profiles.

claim: Duplicates' tendency to cross-bind their own promoters may suggest that interactions between duplicates have evolved to confer beneficial dynamic properties not achieved by a single TF.
source: Duplicates' tendency to cross-bind their own promoters may suggest that interactions between duplicates have evolved to confer beneficial dynamic properties not achieved by a single TF (Teichmann and Babu, 2004; Chapal et al., 2019; Lehner, 2010).
evidence: The claim is a speculative statement supported by citations to published literature (Teichmann and Babu, 2004; Chapal et al., 2019; Lehner, 2010).

claim: TF binding is necessary for gene regulation, but not sufficient.
source: Finally, we note that although TF binding is necessary for gene regulation, it is not sufficient.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Diverging binding preferences are not always translated into changes in transcriptional activity.
source: Hence, diverging binding preferences are not always translated into changes in transcriptional activity.
evidence: The claim is a reasoning statement based on the knowledge that binding is necessary but not sufficient for regulation.
